Aldabra Atoll is the world's second-largest coral atoll - after Kiritimati (Christmas Island). It is part of the Outer Islands (Seychelles) in the Indian Ocean. Aldabra Island is located 1120 km (700 mi) southwest of Victoria (Mahe Island). The Aldabra Atoll has 4 larger islands, plus 40 smaller ones, all inside its lagoon. There are also a few very small islets located between Grand-Terre Island and Picard Islands.

A scientific research station of SIF (Seychelles Islands Foundation) is based at La Gigi village, Picard Island. The permanent staff of 12 people conduct research to study the biodiversity of Aldabra.

Aldabra is not easy to access. No helipads, landing jetties or airstrips, have been permitted to be constructed on the atoll. The closest airfield on Assumption is 50 km (31 ml) south-east of Picard. Supply ships that operate from Mahe provide food and other essentials to the scientists and staff at the station once per 2 months.

Cruises are operated by several cruise lines along with dive boats that may call on Aldabra Atoll on expedition tours. Visits by people other than SIF scientists and staff are strictly controlled. Only guided tours are offered with prior permission and current numbers indicate that an average of 900 tourists are able to see the atoll per year. Within Aldabra, paved walking paths exist from La Gigi village which leads to premonitory from where views of the mangrove species and the large lagoon (during low tides) are seen.

  • Aldabra was designated UNESCO World Heritage Site on November 19, 1982. it is among Seychelles' two UNESCO World Heritage Sites and is managed and protected by SIF. The marine protected area extends 1 km (0.62 ml) into the sea to ensure preservation of the marine fauna. Eco tourism is controlled; introduction of invasive species is restricted.
  • BirdLife International declared Aldabra Atoll as an IBA (Important Endemic Bird Area) in 2001 on account of the atoll's large seabird colonies.
  • In 2010 Aldabra Atoll became Ramsar Wetland Site of International Importance.
  • Aldabra was designated as a site under IOSEA (Indian Ocean South East Asia) turtle network, in the 2014 convention.

Aldabra is not a conventional cruise port. There is no cruise terminal, harbour, jetty, road network or independent tourist infrastructure. Expedition ships visit this remote UNESCO-listed nature reserve under prior authorisation from the Seychelles Islands Foundation (SIF), normally anchoring in the designated area off Picard Island. Passengers go ashore or join water activities in the ship's expedition boats or Zodiacs.

Independent sightseeing is not permitted. Access is limited to designated visitor areas, and activities are supervised by SIF staff. For cruise passengers, the practical approach is to participate in the ship's organised expedition programme rather than attempt to arrange anything independently.

At a Glance

  • Port type: Expedition anchorage; no cruise terminal or pier.
  • Going ashore: By expedition boat or Zodiac, usually to Settlement Beach beside the Aldabra Research Station on Picard Island.
  • Independent access: Not permitted; visitors must remain within approved tourism areas and be accompanied by SIF staff.
  • Transport ashore: No taxis, buses, rental vehicles or public transport.
  • Main activities: Guided nature walks, Zodiac lagoon cruises, snorkelling, supervised beach swimming and, on suitably equipped expedition cruises, scuba diving.
  • Main constraint: Tides strongly control landing times, lagoon access and snorkelling conditions.

Getting from the Ship

Visiting vessels use a designated anchorage near the SIF Research Station on Picard Island. There is no dock, so passengers transfer by small expedition craft. Settlement Beach in front of the research station is the normal landing point. If conditions there are unsuitable, La Gigi in the West Channels may be used instead.

Picard cannot normally be reached by boat around low tide because the fringing reef becomes too shallow. Landing schedules are therefore planned around the local tide, and the day's programme can change at short notice because of currents, wind or sea conditions.

Passengers going ashore also undergo strict biosecurity procedures. Clothing, footwear and equipment must be clean and free of seeds, soil and other material that could introduce invasive species.

Best Ways to Spend Your Time

Guided Nature Walk on Picard Island

This is the main land-based experience and the best opportunity to see Aldabra's giant tortoises, seabirds, unusual vegetation and raised-coral landscape. All routes begin near the Research Station and are guided.

  • La Gigi walk: About 1 hour round trip. A relatively short coastal walk on a sandy path toward the lagoon, with views across Passe Femme and opportunities to watch frigatebirds, boobies and other seabirds.
  • Historical walk: Up to about 1 hour 30 minutes. Follows the coast toward the remains of the former settlement, including old buildings, water tanks, a church and cemetery.
  • Backpath walk: About 1 hour. A more natural route behind the station through vegetation and across exposed fossil coral. The terrain is rougher and the walk is considered moderately difficult.

Picard and the Research Station area are the only terrestrial parts of the atoll normally open to visitors. Landing elsewhere is prohibited.

Zodiac Cruise Through the Lagoon

A lagoon cruise is one of the most practical ways to experience Aldabra because much of the wildlife and landscape is best viewed from the water. Trips are timed around high tide and follow approved routes with SIF staff aboard.

The shorter West Channels cruise generally takes about 1–2 hours, passing mangroves, coral islets and narrow tidal channels. A longer trip between the Main Channel and West Channels may take around 2–3 hours and can provide sightings of turtles, rays, sharks, wading birds, boobies and frigatebirds.

Snorkelling

Snorkelling may be offered on the outer reef or in selected tidal channels. Some locations are used for drift snorkelling, so this is a controlled expedition activity rather than independent swimming from shore.

Currents can be strong and vary rapidly with the tide. Expedition staff and SIF personnel assess conditions before guests enter the water, and channel snorkels are normally arranged so the current carries swimmers toward the lagoon rather than out to sea. Participation requirements depend on conditions and the expedition team's safety assessment.

Beach Swimming near the Research Station

When conditions allow, passengers may spend some time on Settlement Beach and swim close to shore under supervision. Blacktip reef sharks are frequently present in the shallows and are one of the notable wildlife sightings here. Swimmers must remain within the area specified by expedition and SIF staff.

Scuba Diving

Some expedition vessels arrange diving in designated areas including Settlement, Anse Var and selected channels. Diving must be organised in advance with SIF and requires qualified expedition dive staff as well as SIF supervision.

Currents are a significant factor. Main Channel is particularly demanding and is reserved for experienced divers with the appropriate certification and skills. Diving should therefore be considered an expedition activity rather than something passengers can arrange locally after arrival.

Walking and Terrain

There is no self-guided walking tour at Aldabra. Visitors must remain with their assigned group and guide. Even the shorter walks can involve sand, exposed coral, uneven natural paths, heat and little conventional visitor infrastructure. Passengers with reduced mobility should discuss suitability with the expedition team before going ashore.

The La Gigi route is generally the easiest choice for passengers wanting a shorter outing. The Backpath is more uneven, while the longer historical route requires more sustained walking.

Practical Tips

  • Expect the day's programme to be built around tides rather than a fixed sightseeing timetable.
  • Follow the ship's biosecurity instructions carefully before landing; dirty footwear or equipment can delay or prevent going ashore.
  • There are no normal tourist facilities, restaurants, shops, taxis or independently bookable tours on the atoll.
  • Facilities ashore are extremely limited, so most passengers return to the ship between major activities.
  • Do not leave marked routes, approach wildlife independently or collect shells, coral or other natural material.
  • Weather, currents and tide height may require activities to be shortened, moved or cancelled.
  • Keep closely to the expedition team's return instructions. Small-boat access across the reef is tide-dependent, making independent delays particularly impractical.
